My aunt Vesna keeps the accordion shop on Vrbnik Street, the one my grandfather opened with a borrowed lathe and a hand-painted sign he made twice, because the first one leaned. I spent July at the low bench under the window, holding parts while she named them. On the bench between us lay the instrument she had promised for the end of the month. It belonged to a nine-year-old on Petrinja Street whose mother had traded a winter of piecework for it. The girl would learn on it, badly, for years. Her teacher had asked only that the buttons be easy under a small hand, and that nothing on it be worth crying over.

"We build it forgiving, this one," Vesna said. "She will drop it. She will leave it beside a radiator. Everything we do has to survive a child who does not love it yet." So she fitted the straps a size short so that they could be let out later, and she left the dent in the grille where it had always been, because a scratch on a scratched thing costs a child nothing.

The instrument lay open the way something lies open on a surgeon's table: bellows folded back, reed blocks lifted out and stood in rows on a square of felt. Vesna worked without hurrying. She kept a chalk line down the middle of the bench, and everything she had touched went to her side of it. I found a reed that buzzed and swapped it for the sweetest one in the tin box of salvaged reeds on the shelf. Vesna lifted my reed out again, fitted a plainer one, and screwed the block down. "A beginner has to hear her own mistakes," she said. "Give her honey and she will never learn to listen." Then she packed the case in a canvas bag with a spare strap in the pocket. When the girl came for it she played four notes, every one of them wrong, and Vesna smiled as though the month had ended exactly on time.

In the spring of 1903 the harbor commission of Alder Cove, a fishing port of nine hundred people, met to settle a question it had deferred for six years. Hollis Vane, the engineer the town had hired the previous autumn, laid his plan before the seven commissioners: to cut a second entrance through the sand spit at Low Point, so that vessels need not beat around the shoal in a southerly wind. His estimate was fourteen thousand dollars, more than Alder Cove had ever borrowed at one time. When the meeting opened, the standing motion was the merchant Amos Kerr's, to do the work in stages over ten years and borrow nothing. Two commissioners, Pell and Danforth, had said nothing at all.

What moved them was neither Vane's drawings nor his figures. A letter came from an Army engineer at the district office, undertaking to match, dollar for dollar, whatever Alder Cove itself spent on the cut. Fourteen thousand dollars had suddenly become seven, and Pell and Danforth voted with Vane that evening.

Kerr's answer was not that the work was useless. It was that the district office had given two other towns the same undertaking within his memory and had honored it in neither of them. He lost, five to two, and the town borrowed in June.

The town dug its own half of the cut in 1904 and stopped. The federal money arrived in 1912 and came to less than a third of the sum promised. The entrance was opened to nine feet and never to the fifteen Vane had drawn; vessels used it in fair weather and avoided it in foul. Whether it would have answered at full depth cannot be said. Vane left in 1908 for a larger post, and the minute book gives the whole business one line.

Marta Sandoval spent thirty years compiling the first dictionary of the dialect of the high mountain province, working at a kitchen table between teaching posts. What happened to those finished pages is still argued about in the valleys she recorded. No volume of her own was ever bound, and she never paid a printer anything at all. The university library asked twice for the manuscript, and she had still not answered when the slips left for the capital; nothing reached the library. A newspaper offered to print one letter of the alphabet a month, and she refused to let the work appear in parts. A compiler in the capital borrowed her slips for a summer, and eleven thousand of her entries stand in his national dictionary under his name. A publisher across the border wanted a translation, but nothing of hers appeared abroad in any language.

One market day a week for nineteen years she stood among the stalls asking sellers what they called things, certain that people speak most truly while haggling over goods. She began each market day with the same question, the old name for a measure of oil, and set down whatever the first stall told her. A word went onto a card the first time a seller said it, without waiting for a second mouth. Parish books and wills she never opened, holding that a word owes nothing to having once been written down. The village teachers offered to have their classes write to her, and she refused: a child's page reaches the post already corrected. She kept no correspondents in other villages, saying that one market draws twelve villages to it, so postbags were waste.

Her name appears nowhere in his three volumes, not even among the thanks. It is no comedy, and hardly a waste, since the words did survive; her stubbornness is not the point, and impatience would be misplaced. The feeling the story leaves is indignation on her behalf, at a theft nobody has yet called one.

Kellerman's yard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. The launch Marisol stood on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her; Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life. By Monday every house on the lake had a use to propose for her; by Friday she had a new owner. The marina at Two Harbours sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank. The sailing club had asked in June to teach beginners in her; he said a gift clears no debt, and no beginner boarded her. He had pushed a knife into her garboard plank in June; it went in no quarter inch, and no rot showed along her keel. The islanders would take the county's new boat; the crossing, he said, was no longer his. Petrus rowed over to trade his skiff and outboard; Teodor, who could still slip her single-handed, said a swap brings no money through the gate.

The bank had carried the mortgage since the bad winter, and the sum owed had grown past what a season of repairs could earn. Every other use proposed that week ended at the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would not open again. “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”

The sale drew half the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried chairs out for people I had never met. He never asked the registry to put her name back on the list. I was not relieved, I was not proud of him, and nothing in it struck me as funny. There would be no crossing to dread in January; I was angry with him all evening, and knew even then the anger was unfair, since the cheque was the yard's one chance.

Grieve's Salt Line was made in 1961, dropped after two seasons, and revived this month by the Vellacott company in a better version. Five changes are credited with the improvement: the casting of older dancers; the slower tempo of the score; the cutting of the third section; the restored side-lighting; the move to a smaller house. One of them does the work.

It is the tempo. Taken a third slower, the crossing steps land on the breath, and the dancers stop fighting the music. The lighting comes from overhead as before, and no shadow falls. The company is young, and the hesitations still read as error. The third section survives entire, argument and all. The house seats two thousand, and every gesture must be enlarged.

The score was recopied from the 1961 parts, and two errors in it corrected. Twenty dancers were never seen at any audition here. The boards are unmarked, and no scratch shows where the set stood. Nothing is unsettled between the company and the estate. No usher tallies the empty seats, ruled book or otherwise.

Grieve's programme note of 1961 is reprinted in the new booklet. The note leaves the tempo to the conductor, which is why the company may take it as slow as it likes. Lighting is fixed there too, the house given no say. It wants dancers of sixty, grey heads at that. The third section it calls the heart of the piece. The smallest room is what it asks for.

Restore the old tempo and the evening collapses; nothing else on that list is holding it up, so nothing else would save it. I have nothing to qualify: go, and take somebody who dislikes dance. Those dancers could give it nightly for a year; I wonder nothing. I have always liked the piece, and my liking was never questioned. The piece was never in danger of being lost; no rescue was needed. The applause is no louder than the evening warrants, and fashion explains nothing.

Bell Ridge holds an old aspen clone that renewed itself each spring until, in the 1980s, its new shoots stopped surviving the summer. Five explanations have circulated since: elk browsing the shoots off; salt from the winter road; a canker under the bark; a spell of dry years; shade from the crowding firs. Sandoval's crew spent four summers deciding among them.

The evidence is for salt: the soil below the culvert tests four times saltier than the ridge, and the failures crowd that band. Nothing here was bitten; the elk stay down in the meadow. No canker showed when bark was opened at forty trunks. The failure began in the wettest decade the valley records. The firs are no denser now, and noon light reaches the ground.

A cold spring runs below the boundary rock, and the crew fill their bottles there. Sandoval oversees nothing here; the warden manages the ridge. Nothing stretches along a line; the plots are one flat acre. Nobody moves at speed on that slope, where the counting is slow. No machine operates in the stand; the crew carry one tape.

Photographs from the same rock each August have been kept since 1946. What they supply is a date: the bare verge first shows in the frame for 1971. They give no height; the shoots fall below the frame. The trunks show as blurs, and their bark cannot be judged. The creek hides behind the rock, so no water is gauged. The fir line stands beyond the frame and cannot be followed.

The cure follows the cause: flush the salt out and the shoots return. Nothing else on the list is at fault, so nothing else would work. The work is good, though I would take care carrying it beyond this ridge. I will not praise this without hedging. I doubt neither the method nor its conclusion. I make no complaint of delay; the four summers were well spent. I take it for no small matter, and tidy is wrong.

The mayfly hatch on Lake Ferrin once darkened the village streetlights for a week each June, and it has not done so since 2011. Five causes have been proposed: perch stocked for anglers, a dam trapping the silt the nymphs burrow in, fertilizer running off the lakeside farms, a raised weir drowning the shallows, and water warmer than before. Three summers of survey work point one way.

The surveys point to the dam. The silt the nymphs burrow in has not passed it since 2009, and the bed below is bare gravel. The stocked perch eat no nymphs, their stomachs holding snails. No algae bloom has formed; the farms' runoff stays low. The weir was never raised; its boards sit as in 1950. The lake runs no warmer than it did, June for June.

A spring feeds the north bay, a source of cold water all summer. Nothing climbs in that season; the shallows stay cold. The gauge holds no coil, working by float and chain. No trout leap for flies here, the lake having none. The trouble has no single origin anyone has found. The club's catch book dates the last big hatch to June of 2010. No change in the fishing appears there after the stocking. No members are named in it, only weights and dates. The catch book records no weather of any kind. No boast about the fishing is preserved there.

Return depends on passing silt below the dam, which a sluice could manage. Taking the perch out would gain nothing; the nymphs are safe from them. A buffer strip along the farms would catch runoff that never comes. Lowering the weir boards would uncover shallows never drowned. Cooler summers would help nothing, the lake being cool enough.

The club's conduct puzzles me; it paid for the survey and then ignored it. The club's conduct earns no praise from me. Its conduct rouses no anger in me. No hope comes to me from the club's conduct. Indifference is not what the club's conduct meets from me.
